title: Fabry-Perot Narrowband Transmission Filter for 1550 nm LiDAR
scientific_hypothesis: A symmetric Fabry-Perot cavity with quarter-wave Bragg mirrors surrounding a half-wave defect layer will achieve peak transmittance at 1550 nm while creating stopbands at 1400-1500 nm and 1600-1700 nm, with performance improving as mirror pair count increases up to the 30-layer constraint.
design_principle: Recalled thin-film optics: alternating high/low index layers at quarter-wave optical thickness create a photonic bandgap. Inserting a half-wave defect layer in the center creates a transmission resonance within the stopband. The number of mirror pairs controls stopband width and depth; the defect layer thickness controls the resonance wavelength.
proposed_topology: Air | (Ta2O5/SiO2)_7 | Ta2O5 | (SiO2/Ta2O5)_7 | Fused Silica substrate - 29 layers total: 14 mirror pairs plus 1 defect layer, starting with high-index layer from air side
design_variables: individual layer thicknesses for all 29 layers
defect layer thickness specifically tuned for 1550 nm resonance
manufacturing_considerations: total layer count fixed at 29 to stay under 30-layer limit
quarter-wave layers should be near 100-300 nm thickness range at 1550 nm for practical deposition
theory_basis: Recalled: Quarter-wave stack reflectance increases with number of layer pairs, approximately R = ((nH/nL)^(2N) - 1) / ((nH/nL)^(2N) + 1) for N pairs
Recalled: Fabry-Perot transmission peak occurs when defect layer optical thickness equals integer multiples of half-wavelength
Recalled: Stopband width scales with refractive index contrast ratio nH/nL
Recalled: Ta2O5 has higher refractive index (~2.1-2.2) than SiO2 (~1.44-1.45) at 1550 nm, providing good contrast for Bragg mirrors
Recalled: Symmetric mirror structure around defect layer produces cleaner transmission profile than asymmetric designs
expected_advantages: High peak transmittance achievable with sufficient mirror pairs
Well-defined stopbands on both sides of 1550 nm
Symmetric design simplifies optimization and reduces sensitivity to thickness errors
All 29 layers can be individually tuned during optimization rounds
known_risks: Ta2O5 refractive index value at 1550 nm is recalled as approximately 2.1-2.2 but exact value uncertain - registry dataset will provide measured data
SiO2 refractive index recalled as ~1.44-1.45 at 1550 nm but exact value uncertain - registry dataset will provide measured data
7 mirror pairs per side may not provide sufficient stopband depth for 1400-1500 nm and 1600-1700 nm suppression - may need to verify if 29 layers is enough
Angle of incidence not specified in request - assuming normal incidence (0 degrees) but LiDAR receivers may have finite field of view
Polarization not specified - design assumes unpolarized or normal incidence where polarization splitting is minimal
Exact passband width around 1550 nm not defined - optimization will naturally determine bandwidth based on mirror pair count
Material absorption in Ta2O5 at 1550 nm not accounted for in recalled knowledge - extinction coefficient data from registry will determine if this matters
execution_request_english: Design a planar multilayer dielectric filter for 1550 nm LiDAR receiver. Incident medium is Air. Substrate is Fused Silica. Use exactly 29 layers with materials Ta2O5 (Gao) and SiO2 (Lemarchand). Stack structure: Air | (Ta2O5 (Gao)/SiO2 (Lemarchand))_7 | Ta2O5 (Gao) | (SiO2 (Lemarchand)/Ta2O5 (Gao))_7 | Fused Silica. Optimize all 29 layer thicknesses to maximize transmittance at 1550 nm while minimizing transmittance in 1400-1500 nm and 1600-1700 nm bands. Wavelength bands for evaluation: 1400-1500 nm (suppression), 1550 nm (transmission peak), 1600-1700 nm (suppression). Normal incidence assumed. Total layer count fixed at 29. Materials: Ta2O5 (Gao) (high index), SiO2 (Lemarchand) (low index).
